items.title: The Spinning Jenny multiplied a worker's output eightfold
items.claim: What did James Hargreaves invent around 1764?

options.text: The Spinning Jenny — a multi-spindle frame allowing one operator to spin eight (later up to 120) threads at once; patented 1770, transformed cotton production

items.reveal:
Hargreaves, a Lancashire weaver, named the device after his daughter (or wife) Jenny. Early versions had 8 spindles; later models up to 120. Cotton output per worker rose dramatically.

The jenny was joined by Richard Arkwright's water frame (1769, water-powered) and Samuel Crompton's mule (1779, combining both). Edmund Cartwright's power loom (1785) mechanised weaving. Eli Whitney's cotton gin (1793) mechanised seed-removal in the US South — increasing cotton supply and intensifying slavery.

Lancashire became the centre of world cotton manufacture by 1830, employing perhaps half a million workers by mid-century. Cotton's raw material came largely from the slave plantations of the US South until the American Civil War.
items.why: The Industrial Revolution was a sequence of specific machines invented by specific people, each enabling the next. 'Cotton' is shorthand for a chain of innovation that links Lancashire mills to plantation slavery.

items.title: The Berlin Wall fell partly because of a press-conference error
items.claim: How did the Berlin Wall come to open on 9 November 1989?

options.text: Soviet troops dismantled it overnight on Gorbachev's orders

East German official Günter Schabowski announced new travel rules at a 6 p.m. press conference; asked when they took effect, he said 'as far as I know, immediately'; East Berliners massed at checkpoints and crossings opened without orders
Mass armed insurrection overwhelmed border guards
West German forces breached the wall by force

items.reveal:
The East German politburo had agreed new travel rules on 9 November 1989, intended to take effect the following day with bureaucratic processing. Schabowski had not been briefed in detail. Asked by Italian journalist Riccardo Ehrman 'when does this take effect?', he shuffled papers and said 'Sofort, unverzüglich' — immediately, without delay.

Within hours East Berliners gathered at the Bornholmer Strasse crossing. Commander Harald Jäger received no orders and, faced with thousands of citizens, opened the barrier around 11.30 p.m.

Within months the regime collapsed. German reunification followed on 3 October 1990. The Soviet Union itself dissolved on 26 December 1991.
items.why: Major historical turning points can hinge on a botched press conference. The Wall's opening was not authorised in the way it happened — it was triggered by a misstatement that the crowd then made real.

items.title: The Korean War killed around 3 million people
items.claim: What was the death toll of the Korean War (June 1950-July 1953)?

options.text: Estimates centre around 3 million dead, mostly Korean civilians; nearly 37,000 US, around 1,000 British and Commonwealth, and over 400,000 Chinese troops killed
Comparable to WWI losses for the Allies

items.reveal:
North Korea invaded south of the 38th parallel on 25 June 1950. UN forces under General MacArthur landed at Inchon (September 1950) and pushed to the Yalu River; China entered in October-November.

The armistice was signed at Panmunjom on 27 July 1953. There has never been a peace treaty — the two Koreas are still technically at war. Pyongyang was reduced by US bombing to perhaps 25% of its buildings; an estimated 20% of North Korea's population died.

In the US, sandwiched between WWII and Vietnam, it became 'the forgotten war' despite high casualties.
items.why: Conflict casualties are not just about combatant deaths. Korea's civilian toll, the bombing intensity and the legacy of an unresolved war shape East Asia today — but rarely feature in Cold War textbooks.
